articles.summary: Truce begins in wartorn Ukraine city after it was announced by Melania Trump  BBCUkraine war latest: Starlink access restored in Ukraine - as Kyiv's forces 'posing long-term threat' to Russia  Sky NewsUkrainian who fled Oleshky views US-brokered ceasefire with deep scepticism  ReutersRussia open to local truces but will not stop offensive  RTE.ieRussia Accuses Ukraine of Launching Strikes Against Oleshky Ahead of Ceasefire  The Moscow Times
articles.full_text:
A truce has begun in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, a week after it was announced by US First Lady, Melania Trump.
The ceasefire is meant to allow aid deliveries and the evacuation of civilians.
Russia's defence ministry said on Telegram it had stopped firing toward the Ukrainian city of Kherson - across the river from Oleshky - at 04:00 Moscow time (01:00 GMT) in preparation for the humanitarian operation.
Oleshky is on the south bank of the river Dnipro, which forms the front line in the Kherson region. The remaining residents have been desperately short of food and other essential supplies.
Ukraine's parliament commissioner for human rights, Dmytro Lubinets, confirmed in a social media post that the ceasefire had begun.
"As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honouring its commitments," he wrote on Facebook.
Oleshky was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Residents were trapped with scarce food between Ukrainian positions across the Dnipro River and Russian forces to the east.
The city was home to 24,000 people before the war. Now Ukraine estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children.
The White House said last week that Melania Trump had secured the ceasefire in Oleshky.
"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," she said in a press release.
While the US first lady is relatively lower profile than some of her predecessors - and only occasionally seen at White House events - she has become involved in addressing humanitarian issues stemming from the Russia-Ukraine war.
In August 2025, she penned a letter to Putin, telling him it was "time to protect children and future generations worldwide".

articles.title: Kayhan opens fire on diplomacy, warns Iran risks losing leverage - Iran International
articles.summary: Kayhan opens fire on diplomacy, warns Iran risks losing leverage  Iran International
articles.full_text:
As Iran hosted senior Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani officials for security talks on Monday, an influential hardline newspaper editor warned that the diplomatic initiative could undermine Tehran's position and relieve pressure on the United States.
Hossein Shariatmadari, editor of Kayhan daily and a longtime appointee of the late supreme leader Ali Khamenei, questioned the purpose of the gathering in an article headlined “Tehran summit: Oasis or mirage?”
His criticism extended even to Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and himself a prominent hardliner who opposed the nuclear diplomacy of former President Hassan Rouhani.
Bagheri had presented the meeting as an opportunity to develop a new regional security framework. Shariatmadari dismissed that prospect, arguing that Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan were too close to the United States to credibly mediate between Tehran and Washington.
He accused the three countries of supporting US and Israeli military operations against Iran and questioned why Tehran would expect them to abandon their longstanding strategic ties with Washington.
Iran's support for the Houthis
Shariatmadari's central objection concerned Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed the Mecca mutual defense pact in August, committing themselves to collective defense. With Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia intensifying, Shariatmadari argued that cooperation with the three countries risked weakening Iran's support for the Yemeni group.
He described Iran, Hezbollah, the Houthis, Iraqi militias and Palestinian armed factions as “one spirit in several bodies,” arguing that confronting any of them amounted to confronting Iran itself.
Shariatmadari questioned whether the visiting delegations intended to pressure Tehran into distancing itself from the Houthis and insisted Iran would never abandon them.
Yet he also portrayed the diplomatic visit as evidence of Iranian strength, arguing that the closure of the Strait of Hormuz had brought Washington and its allies close to economic suffocation and forced regional governments to seek relief through Tehran.
His argument exposed a tension in the hardline position: the arrival of foreign delegations was presented as proof that Iran's pressure was succeeding, while negotiations aimed at easing that pressure risked squandering the leverage it had created.
Against compromise
On Saturday, the hardline Paydari Front urged Iran to begin withdrawing from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty and reconsider its defense doctrine. Hardline lawmakers have also sought to impeach Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi over his dealings with Washington.
These critics are closely tied to Iran's security establishment. Paydari Front leader Sadegh Mahsouli is a former Revolutionary Guards officer, while Shariatmadari represented the late supreme leader at Kayhan for decades.
Their criticism has continued even as President Masoud Pezeshkian and national security chief Mohsen Rezaei welcomed the visiting delegations. The four countries ended Monday's meeting with an agreement to continue discussions on regional peace and security.
The dispute exposes a growing divide within Iran's ruling establishment over what to do with the leverage created by months of confrontation.
Shariatmadari and like-minded hardliners believe that confrontation is working. In their view, diplomacy that requires Tehran to relinquish that leverage risks trading away the very gains it has produced.

articles.title: North Korean agents are infiltrating Western businesses by posing as employees, security chief warns - The European Magazine
articles.summary: North Korean agents are infiltrating Western businesses by posing as employees, security chief warns  The European Magazine
articles.full_text:
State sponsored hackers from North Korea and other hostile states are using fake identities, manipulated video interviews and stolen passwords to gain access to Western businesses. And thanks to AI, their methods are becoming increasingly sophisticated and difficult to detect, one of the UK’s leading cyber security chiefs has told The European
Cyber criminals are gaining access to company networks by posing as legitimate employees, stealing passwords and exploiting trusted accounts, a leading security expert has warned.
Steve Durbin, chief executive of the Information Security Forum (ISF), said attackers were increasingly using sophisticated deception to gain entry to organisations, sometimes securing jobs under false identities before exploiting their access to sensitive systems.
In an exclusive interview this weekend, he warned that conventional security measures were often ineffective against criminals who had obtained legitimate login credentials.
“Attackers these days don’t tend to break in,” he said. “They log in.”
Durbin highlighted the growing threat from North Korean IT operatives who apply for remote positions using fabricated credentials and manipulated video appearances, potentially securing access to company networks once hired.
“They’re now a trusted insider because you’ve hired them into your organisation,” he said.
The practice has become sufficiently widespread to prompt repeated warnings from the FBI, which reported earlier this month that North Korean operatives were using stolen identities and intermediaries to obtain jobs with Western companies, steal information and extort their employers.
Durbin warned that European businesses employing remote workers were also vulnerable to such tactics, particularly when recruitment and identity checks were conducted entirely online.
Beyond fraudulent recruitment, hackers can gain access to company networks by stealing employee passwords, impersonating legitimate users or exploiting access granted to suppliers, allowing them to move through systems without immediately triggering security alarms.
Once inside, criminals may spend time studying an organisation’s systems, identifying valuable information and disabling backup facilities before launching ransomware attacks or demanding payment to prevent stolen material being published.
AI is making these methods easier and cheaper to deploy, Durbin warned, with criminals increasingly able to purchase ready-made tools for generating convincing fraudulent emails, cloning voices and distributing malicious software.
The consequences, he said, could be particularly serious for organisations responsible for Britain’s electricity, water, healthcare and transport networks.
Durbin identified three factors making critical infrastructure especially vulnerable – outdated systems connected to the internet, the pressure to restore essential services quickly, and hostile governments using criminal groups to conduct attacks on their behalf.
“Nobody wants to be without electricity. Nobody wants to be without water. Nobody wants to be just about to be wheeled into an operating theatre to find that all the systems go down,” he said.
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) handled more than 200 incidents affecting Britain’s critical national infrastructure and its supporting organisations in the year to May 2026, with around three-quarters believed to be linked to hostile state actors.
Speaking to The European’s Juliette Foster, Durbin cited a UK government worst-case assessment suggesting that recovery from a serious cyber attack on the water sector could take several months.
He also described a manufacturer whose factories were brought to a halt after criminals disabled its corporate IT network, despite leaving the factories’ own systems untouched.
His warnings followed widespread precautionary website shutdowns last week after two critical vulnerabilities were discovered in PHP, a programming language used extensively across the internet.
Government bodies, businesses and healthcare organisations were among those affected as security authorities warned that attackers could exploit the flaws to gain unauthorised access to vulnerable systems. Emergency software updates were subsequently released to address the weaknesses.
Durbin said organisations are now spending too much on preventing attacks and too little on preparing for the consequences when their defences failed.
He called for closer cooperation between government and privately owned infrastructure providers, arguing that public-sector procurement and regulation often struggled to keep pace with rapidly developing cyber threats.
And he urged company directors to understand the risks associated with new technologies before committing substantial sums to AI projects, particularly during difficult economic conditions.
“They’re using AI just like we are. And it’s the as a service piece that really worries me the most because that removes the need for the attacker to be hugely sophisticated,” he added.
Watch the full interview with Steve Durbin, chief executive of the Information Security Forum, on The European’s YouTube channel.

By
Andrea Margolis, Fox News
Published Oct. 26, 2026, 7:20 p.m. PT
See more of our coverage in your search results.

The U.S. State Department has updated travel advisories for several Middle Eastern countries, warning of potential armed attacks by Iranian-backed Houthi forces and threats targeting Americans.
Five countries — Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Syria and Yemen — are listed under the department’s highest advisory level, Level 4, which warns Americans not to travel.
Eight others, including Israel, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, are designated Level 3, urging travelers to reconsider their plans.
While the advisory levels largely remained unchanged, all 13 advisories were updated on Friday.
The advisories cited recent attacks by Iranian-supported Houthis, including strikes on Riyadh’s airport in Saudi Arabia and “other critical infrastructure,” the department said.
The attacks have resulted in civilian deaths and widespread travel disruptions, with the State Department warning that the hostilities “have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area.”
Americans traveling to the region also face additional risks, including health concerns in Iraq and Yemen, officials said.
Kidnapping and hostage-taking were listed as additional concerns in Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Syria and Yemen, according to the State Department.
Civil unrest was also cited as a risk in Iran, Iraq, Israel, Lebanon, Syria and Yemen.
The State Department encourages Americans traveling to these countries to enroll in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP) to receive security alerts and updates from U.S. embassies.
Americans are also urged to monitor local news, prepare to shelter in place if conditions worsen and have an emergency departure plan that does not rely on U.S. government assistance.
Fox News Digital reached out to the State Department for additional information.
The updates follow several other recent travel warnings issued by the State Department.
Last week, the State Department raised its travel advisory for Kenya from Level 2, “Exercise Increased Caution,” to Level 3, “Reconsider Travel,” citing health risks, crime, civil unrest, kidnapping and terrorism.
At around the same time, officials warned Americans traveling to China of the risk of wrongful detention, electronic surveillance and restrictions that could prevent them from leaving the country.

articles.title: Europe feels strain of war in Ukraine - The Statesman
articles.summary: Europe feels strain of war in Ukraine  The Statesman
articles.full_text:
A student dormitory, two medical facilities and transport infrastructure were damaged in the October 26 assault. Nine injured people were hospitalised, according to Kyiv authorities.
The continuing war in Ukraine is placing strain not only on Kyiv but also on Europe, especially since it assumed the sole responsibility to fund Ukraine. President Donald Trump reduced financial support to Ukraine seeking to push Kyiv into accepting a peace deal more suited to Russia than itself. President Volodymyr Zelenskky refused, though he appears to be bending now. Inputs mention that since January 2025, US support to Ukraine has reduced from $130 billion, during the tenure of President Joe Biden, to $540 million now.
The US desires that Europe purchase military equipment for supporting Ukraine from US manufacturers. In end 2024, just prior to the conclusion of his presidency, Biden approved provision of artillery ammunition, rockets and armoured vehicles for Ukraine. He also released a $1.25 billion aid package. Europe was aware that Trump coming into the White House would imply cuts in aid to Ukraine. This happened. Trump had stated during his electioneering, “You (Zelenskky) should have never started it (war). You could have made a deal.” Trump recently mentioned, “The United States has spent a fortune. Europe has spent a fortune. Europe’s tired of it right now.”
Advertisement
Trump believes Zelenskky is prolonging the war due to financial and military support Ukraine receives from Europe. For Europe, Ukraine is a frontline state, defending it from Russian expansionism, despite President Vladimir Putin stating on multiple occasions that he has no such intention. In a recent interview Putin termed this belief of Europe as “some kind of political schizophrenia”. On 16 October, during an EU summit, Zelenskky announced that the war in 2027 would cost Ukraine an additional €155 billion. He therefore re queste d EU for an additional €70 billion loan, in addition to a previously released €90 billion. These were to be utilized for defence, weapon production and national resilience. Ukraine is forced to bank on support from Europe.
Advertisement
Europe made no commitment to fund Ukraine’s additional demand. Europe has been funding Ukraine through a combination of market borrowings, utilizing interest from frozen Russian central bank assets to structure loans, and specific defence production programmes. To meet additional funding demands, Europe is considering either enhancing joint debt, increase national budget grants or exploit Russia’s frozen assets. The earlier amount of €90 billion was accepted on the assumption that the war would conclude in 2026. That does not seem to be happening.
Europe has not been able to exploit the €210 billion in frozen Russian assets held largely by the Central Security Depository Euroclear in Belgium due to blocks by members. The US has been proposing that Europe release some part of frozen Russian assets back to Russia to encourage a peace deal, which the Europeans are unwilling to accept. Within the EU there are questions on continuing support for Ukraine. Hungary, the Czech Republic and Slovakia have refused to join the funding of the €90 billion package to Ukraine. Bulgaria announced that it would no longer contribute towards procurement of new lethal weapons for Ukraine. Their reasons are varying.
Europe will also face a series of elections in 2027 which could impede support to Ukraine. While Spain has elections in end November, Poland, Italy, France, Estonia, Finland, Greece and Slovakia go to polls next year. In all these countries there are political parties exploiting funding for Ukraine for gaining brownie points. Marine Le Pen, the challenger in France, commented recently, “This funding will stop, and it is a matter of honesty to tell (Zelenskky) the truth.” She has also called for an end to Europe’s sanctions on Russia. In Germany, the growing political party, AfD (Alternate for Germany), is demanding restoration of energy ties with Russia.
It also believes support for Ukraine is ‘self-sabotaging.’ A similar scenario is emerging in Italy and Poland. The EU is compelled to approach non-EU nations like Canada, UK, Norway and Japan to join the funding plan. Simultaneously, Europe is backing a ceasefire in Ukraine. Meanwhile large parts of Europe are facing protests over multiple issues including low education funding, high costs of living, soaring fuel and energy costs, housing shortages and declining public services. Added to this is growing frustration over sponsoring multi-billion military and financial packages for Ukraine. There is a belief that these funds could have been better utilized for domestic needs. This internal pressure will continue and possibly be fuelled by outside sources, who are aware that they can influence Europe’s determination to support Ukraine.
Euronews mentions that while there is no evidence that foreign powers fuelled riots in Europe, there is a belief that they exploited it to push their own narratives. The Italian and French governments have tasked their intelligence agencies to investigate whether Russian agents or online networks linked to Russia stoked local unrest. Simultaneously, US pressure on Zelenskky mounts, especially after the 9 October conversation between Trump and Putin. Speeds of Starlink and Starshield were reduced, restricting Ukraine’s ability to defend itself. It has since been restored.
US equipment supplies have slowed to a trickle. Intelligence sharing comes in spurts and the US has agreed to a diesel deal with Russia , while lifting sanctions. Zelenskky accused the US of preventing European nations from transferring their Patriot stocks to it. Zelenskky has seen the writing on the wall. In an interview with multiple channels, he now says he is open to a deal which involves freezing of frontlines. He mentioned, “Right now, we have to freeze, and I think this is a real way to end this war.” The reason he gave was, “Of course, we are not losing this war. But we are losing people.” Russia is exploiting the scenario in Europe. While it backs trilateral talks involving the US and Ukraine commencing post 10th November (after the US mid-term election results), it is unwilling to agree to a ceasefire. It continues its attacks on Ukraine.
Ukraine is responding by strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, targeting just what Trump seeks to avoid. There are also reports that Putin has slowed repairs of Russian refineries damaged by Ukraine, thus keeping oil prices high, impacting the US midterm elections. Putin is aware that the war would add pressure on European finances as they cannot stop funding Ukraine, especially as the US is out. Support to Ukraine is also being exploited by local opposition political parties and by agents of inimical nations to fuel anger within Europe. There is no easy solution for European leaders.
(The writer is a retired Major-General of the Indian Army.)

articles.title: Pakistan raises interest rate to 12 percent as Middle East war fuels inflation - Arab News PK
articles.summary: Pakistan raises interest rate to 12 percent as Middle East war fuels inflation  Arab News PK
articles.full_text:
- Central bank increases policy rate by half a percentage point as energy, wheat prices push inflation higher
- Business groups warn more expensive borrowing will hurt investment and exports
KARACHI: Pakistan’s central bank raised its benchmark interest rate by half a percentage point to 12 percent on Monday, citing a worsening inflation outlook as the Middle East conflict keeps energy prices high.
The increase, effective Tuesday, resumes monetary tightening after a one percentage point rise in April. The State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) had held its rate at 11.5 percent at its subsequent policy meetings.
September’s annual inflation reached 10.3 percent, above the central bank’s expectations and its medium-term target of 5–7 percent. The SBP said higher energy and wheat prices were major contributors and warned that their effects could spread to other prices.
“The Committee noted that the intensification in the Middle East conflict, and low prospects of its near-term resolution, are keeping global energy prices at persistently elevated levels,” the SBP said in its monetary policy statement.
The bank said the conflict had worsened its inflation outlook even though its forecasts for economic growth and the external account remained broadly unchanged. Nine of the monetary policy committee’s 10 members voted for the half-point increase.
“Considering these developments and the evolving risks, the MPC deemed today’s decision as necessary to keep inflation expectations anchored, contain second-round effects of the ongoing supply shock, and bring inflation within the target range of 5-7 percent,” it said.
The International Monetary Fund projected global inflation of 4.7 percent for 2026 in its October economic outlook, citing higher energy and food prices.
BUSINESSES OPPOSE HIKE
The Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FPCCI) called the rate increase “counterproductive,” saying more expensive loans would weigh on manufacturers and exporters already facing high utility tariffs and operating costs.
“It deals a severe blow to ongoing economic stabilization efforts, dampens industrial expansion, and further erodes the global export competitiveness of Pakistani products in international markets,” FPCCI President Atif Ikram Sheikh said in a statement.
Karachi Chamber of Commerce and Industry President Talat Mahmood also opposed the decision.
“The move will further increase the cost of doing business, discourage private-sector investment and undermine efforts to accelerate economic growth,” he said in a statement.
Shankar Talreja, head of research at Topline Securities, said the increase was in line with market expectations and reflected inflation risks from oil and wheat prices.
“The inflation is getting out of hand,” he said, adding that the SBP was acting to bring it back within its target range.
Yasin Iqbal Kodvavi, director of research at Optimus Capital Management, said the central bank had given no clear indication of its next move, but he did not expect another rate increase, citing fiscal buffers and the tightening already undertaken.
Despite the inflation risks, the SBP kept its forecast for economic growth in fiscal 2026–27 at 3.5–4.5 percent. Large-scale manufacturing output rose 1.9 percent year on year in July and August, which the bank said pointed to a gradual recovery in activity.
Pakistan recorded an $874 million current account deficit in the fiscal year’s first quarter. The central bank expects the full-year deficit to remain between zero and one percent of gross domestic product.
SBP Governor Jameel Ahmad said remittances were now projected to reach $45 billion this fiscal year, up from an earlier estimate of $44 billion. He forecast exports of $32.5 billion–$33 billion and imports of $71 billion.
The bank warned that a further escalation of the conflict or adverse weather could threaten its growth outlook.

articles.summary: Pope’s visit confirmed: ‘I look forward to returning to Latin America’  Vatican NewsPope's South American trip to go ahead as planned after lung cancer surgery  BBCPope in 'good health' and trip to South America will go ahead as planned, Vatican says  Sky NewsVATICAN DISPATCH: Pope Leo returns to duties as questions over Church teaching persist  The Catholic HeraldPope Leo XIV to Send Message to Interreligious Prayer Meeting in Assisi  ACI Africa
articles.full_text:
Vatican News
With less than two weeks to go until his Apostolic Journey to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru, Pope Leo XIV has renewed his “great joy and enthusiasm” to undertake this journey on November 6-17.
A statement released on Monday by the Holy See Press Office confirmed that the journey will take place according to the previously-released schedule.
It said the Pope’s journey will “offer opportunities to strengthen the bonds of communion with the local Churches, encourage the faithful in their mission, and bring a message of faith, hope, and peace to the peoples of Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru, encountering the faith of their peoples, and sharing with them the hope and peace that Christ brings to our world.”
Pope Leo expressed his hopes that the visit to Latin America will strength Christians' commitment to proclaiming the Gospel.
“I am looking forward to returning to the continent where I’ve experienced so many moments of my life,” said the Pope in the statement. “May this journey be an occasion for us to open our hearts to one another, strengthen our communion as brothers and sisters, and renew our commitment to proclaiming the Gospel with joy.”
Regarding the Pope’s recovery from surgery on October 13, the statement said the Holy Father’s recovery “continues to progress, in accordance with the favorable assessments communicated by his medical team.”
“As previously reported, the surgical procedure was successful and without complications. Subsequent medical examinations confirmed that the condition was localized and that no further oncological treatment is necessary,” it added.
The statement noted that Pope Leo has gradually resumed his activities while adjusting his daily schedule in consultation with his doctors “to prioritize his recovery while continuing to fulfill the responsibilities of his ministry.”
“He has maintained important appointments and public engagements, remaining attentive to the needs of each day and allowing for appropriate periods of rest,” it said.
The Pope remains “deeply grateful for the prayers and affection he has received from throughout the world and for the dedicated care of the medical professionals who have accompanied him during his recovery.”
The Holy See Press Office statement went on to refer Dr. Luigi Carbone’s words on the Pope’s recovery.
“Dr. Luigi Carbone confirms that the Holy Father’s recovery after the surgery continues, and the latest medical examinations attest to his good health and favorable clinical condition,” it said. “Based on his current clinical status, as well as the instrumental and laboratory tests performed, there are no contraindications that would prevent him from undertaking his upcoming Apostolic Journey to Latin America as planned. The Pope is following medical recommendations with great care and diligence, and with a deep determination to continue serving the Church.”

articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey are pursuing talks with Tehran while strengthening their military readiness under the terms of the Mecca Defence Alliance.
Senior military and security officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey are holding talks with Iranian officials in Tehran as diplomatic efforts to ease tensions between Iran and the United States continue.
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey are members of the Mecca Defence Alliance, a security alliance established amid regional instability and concerns over threats linked to Iran and its allies.
The three countries have now turned to direct talks with Tehran about regional security, even as the alliance faces growing pressure from attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin are attending the talks in Tehran on Monday, according to Saudi and Iranian officials.
They are reportedly meeting with Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei has described the meeting as a potential step towards establishing cooperative regional security mechanisms.
Speaking at his weekly news conference in Tehran, Baghaei reiterated Iran’s longstanding call for what it describes as "endogenous security," a framework that would rely primarily on the capabilities and interests of regional countries.
The Mecca pact: collective defence against regional threats
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August 2026. Under the pact, an armed attack against one member is considered an attack against all three, requiring the others to provide assistance.
The agreement brings together Saudi Arabia’s financial resources and influence in global energy markets, Pakistan’s nuclear capabilities and Turkey’s advanced defence industry and NATO membership.
Although the agreement was signed amid growing concerns over Iran and its allied groups, Turkish officials have insisted that it is not directed against Tehran or any other specific country.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said in an Aug. 8 interview with Anadolu that the agreement did not identify any country as a common threat. He explained that countries would not be considered targets unless they attacked a signatory.
The agreement has received approval in Pakistan, while Turkey has submitted it to parliament but has yet to complete the ratification process.
Houthi attacks put collective defence to the test
Escalating missile and drone attacks by Yemen’s Houthis against Saudi Arabia have presented the Mecca alliance with its first major test.
At an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Oct. 5, the three countries agreed to move towards implementing their collective defence commitments, including measures to ensure the rapid deployment of agreed military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia.
The commitments were outlined in a joint statement published by Turkey’s Foreign Ministry.
Ankara, however, has drawn a line between supporting Saudi Arabia’s defences and joining offensive military operations against the Houthis inside Yemen.
At an Oct. 8 news conference in Ankara, Fidan said the agreement was defensive and ruled out sending Turkish troops to another country to carry out attacks.
Turkey has instead been assessing possible contributions in areas such as air defence, electronic warfare and technical assistance.
The three nations are therefore pursuing direct engagement with Tehran while strengthening their military readiness under the terms of an alliance designed to deter attacks on its members.
Why engage with Tehran?
Pakistan has played a mediating role between Tehran and Washington in recent months. Saudi Arabia is seeking to contain the threat posed by Houthi attacks on its territory and infrastructure, while Turkey has sought to prevent further regional escalation.
Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Rayed Krimly said in an Oct. 26 post on X that the Tehran visit was part of continued efforts by the Mecca pact countries to reduce tensions and encourage diplomatic solutions.
He said the talks were also intended to support mediation efforts by Qatar and Pakistan.
The Saudi statement suggests that talks with Iran are being pursued alongside the alliance’s defence commitments, rather than necessarily representing a fundamental change in the pact’s purpose.
Military deterrence or regional security?
Tehran’s emphasis on locally driven security arrangements appears, at least in principle, to share some common ground with the Mecca pact’s stated objective of strengthening security cooperation among regional states.
Significant differences remain, however.
Saudi Arabia maintains extensive security ties with the United States, Turkey is a NATO member, and Pakistan continues to pursue defence partnerships with several major powers.
Meanwhile, no agreement on a new joint regional security mechanism has been announced.
Nevertheless, the Tehran meeting highlights a notable development: Three countries that have established a mutual defence alliance in response to mounting regional security threats are now also pursuing direct dialogue with Iran.
The key question is whether this dual approach can have a lasting impact on regional tensions.

articles.title: What Melania Trump’s Oleshky Ceasefire Brokerage Reveals About Modern Crisis Leadership - The Organization for World Peace
articles.summary: What Melania Trump’s Oleshky Ceasefire Brokerage Reveals About Modern Crisis Leadership  The Organization for World Peace
articles.full_text:
The southern Ukrainian front-line city of Oleshky, along the Dnipro River in the Russian-occupied Kherson region, is an area of acute civilian suffering amidst protracted war. The Associated Press noted that this city was captured on the first day of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, with a pre-war population of 24,000 people plummeting to between 1,700 and 2,000 residents. The remaining population is predominantly elderly individuals and approximately 50 children. Conditions deteriorated catastrophically following the June 2023 collapse of the Kakhovka Dam, which flooded around 90 percent of the city. For months, remaining residents have endured infrastructure breakdowns without heat, electricity, running water, or reliable access to medicine and food. On top of this, the city is isolated due to heavily mined roads, burned-out vehicles, and constant aerial bombardment.
In an unprecedented diplomatic development as reported by several news outlets, including the AP, CBS News, and Reuters, US First Lady Melania Trump initiated and coordinated direct negotiations between Russian and Ukrainian leadership to establish a localized, temporary ceasefire in Oleshky. Acting in an official capacity as an exclusive intermediary after learning of the crisis during the UN General Assembly, she helped align both warring parties on operational terms. Under this agreement, Russian forces agreed to halt military actions along the Kherson axis, enabling engineering reconnaissance teams to perform landmine removal prior to the entry of humanitarian convoys delivering essential food, water, and medical aid. Furthermore, the accord establishes a designated safe corridor allowing non-military teams to assist elderly residents and coordinate voluntary civilian evacuations to preferred destinations in either Ukraine or Russia. Welcomed by UN Secretary-General António Guterres, and backed by chief Ukrainian negotiator Dmytro Lubinets and Russian officials, this localized pause demonstrates how targeted diplomatic intervention can temporarily open life-saving relief channels in active combat zones.
While the localized ceasefire in Oleshky brings vital, immediate relief to an imperiled population, reliance on high-profile, ad-hoc personal mediation highlights structural flaws in the global humanitarian framework. Contemporary international crisis management increasingly depends on isolated arrangements that alleviate acute, localized distress, with little attention to the underlying drivers of civilian vulnerability: war.
In the context of the conflict in Ukraine, overarching peace negotiations remain bogged down by broader geopolitical frictions, shifting security alliances, and strategic disputes over military assistance and recent satellite communications access. A central critique of ad-hoc humanitarian interventions is their departure from established multilateral mechanisms, resulting in unpredictable, discretionary corridors of relief rather than mandatory compliance with international humanitarian law as posited by organizations like the International Committee of the Red Cross. Under international conventions, occupying powers bear an explicit legal duty to guarantee that civilian populations under their control receive basic food, medical supplies, and essential life-sustaining services. In this situation, when basic human survival depends on specialized, periodic diplomatic interventions rather than enforceable international obligations, humanitarian access can become dangerously subject to political bargaining and publicity requirements. In other words, relying on private media outlets or temporary bilateral assurances rather than permanent, neutral international monitoring bodies, such as the ICRC or UN observation missions, leaves even so-called safe passageways vulnerable to sudden security breakdowns.
Moreover, executing localized ceasefires in contested combat zones without institutionalized monitoring mechanisms exposes civilians and aid workers to severe operational risks. There are heavy risks in having to navigate people through unexploded ordnance, active drone space, and roadways laced with mines, so the experts who clear these paths must be incredibly thorough, and they themselves must also be careful.
Looking to the future, to transform isolated breakthroughs like the Oleshky agreement into dependable protections, the international community may need to adjust its approach to humanitarian leadership during global crises. Perhaps an element of this structural reform is standardized, internationally protected civilian relief corridors operated under neutral verification protocols. Drawing on the established principles of international peacekeeping and neutrality, these corridors could be overseen by non-combative UN observation teams equipped with mine-clearance protocols, continuous satellite tracking, and pre-negotiated safe zones.
On another note, global crisis leadership must also directly link humanitarian compliance to international economic and diplomatic conditionalities. In other words, sovereign states involved in armed conflict should face diplomatic penalties if they restrict access to essential food, clean water, and medical care for civilian populations, an idea that extends beyond the Russia-Ukraine conflict. There’s a chance that integrating verifiable humanitarian access metrics into bilateral trade agreements, diplomatic relations, and international aid negotiations would establish tangible strategic incentives for warring parties to maintain open humanitarian supply lines, thereby eliminating the temptation to weaponize civilian hardship.
In contrast to an institutionalized protocol, an effort with potential to create change is a multi-tiered approach that empowers local civilian officers and non-governmental actors. That is, developing decentralized civic protection networks that equip local authorities with the legal recognition and communication tools necessary to coordinate home visits or assess medical needs, especially so that spoken aid can at last reach the ground. This might be done through a combination of mandatory compliance enforcement and protected local implementation networks, where the international community can move beyond reactive crisis response and build a sustainable global architecture that guarantees civilian safety across conflict zones.
Even these single-city missions leave hope for humanitarianism at a greater scale, and if this initiative is successful, it demonstrates that life-saving relief remains achievable even amidst the most bitter, front-line hostilities. Still, this breakthrough exposes how modern global governance allows a single individual to call for change, while internationally recognized organizations with long-standing institutional histories struggle to call for immediate aid missions involving highly debated conflict parties. The history of neutrality may have been strategic and successful, but the passage of time must also change the aims of organizations, particularly those that have the authority to spearhead aid out of compassion rather than remaining paralyzed by bureaucratic neutrality in times of intense conflict. In the current state of the world, conflicts happen at such devastating levels that uncertainty and hesitance can cause the preventable suffering of thousands. As teams prepare to enter Oleshky, the world will have to see how this mission proceeds, and whether global institutions can evolve to deliver urgent leadership and action that human survival requires.

articles.summary: Red weather warning issued for Isle of Man coastal overtopping  BBCThree further weather warnings issued  Manx RadioFull list of road closures and worst-hit areas as red weather warning approaches  Isle of Man TodayAt-risk roads to close during red weather warning  3FM Isle of ManRare red weather warning issued  Manx Radio
articles.full_text:
A red weather warning has been issued for the Isle of Man for large waves crashing onto coastal roads.
It is in place for coastal overtopping from 22:00 until 01:00 GMT on Tuesday.
The government has asked people to take the "warning seriously and avoid affected coastal areas."
Senior Meteological Officer at Ronaldsway Met Office, Kirsty Wilding said: "Having received updated computer model data overnight, as well as recording what height the tide was last night, the confidence has increased for tonight's high tide."
What is coastal overtopping?
Wildling said coastal overtopping is essentially the breaking of large waves over the sea walls onto exposed coastal roads and promenades.
"It results in large amounts of sea water being brought onshore as well as some debris, for example seaweed and stones - which can cause damage to cards or leave debris on roads when the tide recedes." she said.
She added the higher the tides and the waves, the greater the amount of sea water taken onshore which, she said "brings a greater risk to the public, as the power of the waves can knock people over."
Futher warnings
Alongside the red warning, an amber one for inner harbor flooding has been issued by forecasters at Ronaldsway Met Office.
"Inner harbour flooding expected around the time of the high tide tonight, with a storm surge in the Irish Sea," it said.
The main areas affected will be:
Ramsey
- West Quay,
- East Quay,
- Parliament Street,
- Dale Street,
- Shipyard Road and
- The banks of River Sulby to Gardener's Lane.
Douglas
- Eastern end of North Quay,
- Old Castletown Road and
- Lake Road.
The Met Office said flood defences should also be deployed for the lowest-lying parts of Castletown Harbour.
In addition, a yellow warning for severe gales will come into force from 18:00 until 06:00 on Tuesday.
Gusts between 50-60 mph (80-96 km/h) are expected widely with up to 65mph (104 km/h) forecast for higher ground exposed coastal areas.
"This may result in fallen branches/ trees and disruption to travel," forecasters said.
Travel disruptions
The Liverpool crossing, which was scheduled for 15:00, left Douglas Harbour earlier at 06:00.
While both Manannan Larne sailings were cancelled.
At Ronaldsway Airport, all scheduled flights are going ahead as planned however, the airport have asked for passengers to arrive two hours early due to the number of disrupted flights taking off today.
Storm Boelo
Over the weekend, Storm Boelo kept teams from the Department of Infrastrucutre busy.
The DOI said crews dealt with 85 fallen trees, 31 flooding incidents, and more than 25 other storm-related call-outs.
Sailings and flights to and from the island were also cancelled.

articles.title: Pakistan issues high-alert advisory over phishing and malware attacks via WhatsApp - Daily Times
articles.summary: Pakistan issues high-alert advisory over phishing and malware attacks via WhatsApp  Daily Times
articles.full_text:
Pakistan’s National Cyber Emergency Response Team (NCERT) issued a high-alert cyber security advisory regarding targeted phishing and malware attacks. Cybersecurity officials warned that malicious actors are exploiting WhatsApp Web, WhatsApp Desktop, and compromised email channels to infect Windows systems. According to the advisory, cybercriminals impersonate government officials and state departments to send infected files disguised as official documents. Consequently, opening these malicious attachments can compromise system security, granting unauthorized actors full administrative access to sensitive official data. Therefore, the agency urges all government personnel and citizens to exercise extreme vigilance online.
Read More: Malware attack: PTA asks WhatsApp users in Pakistan to follow advice
The federal cybersecurity agency warned that infected Windows systems allow attackers to execute remote commands, steal saved passwords, and extract confidential records. Furthermore, hackers can hijack active WhatsApp Web sessions and impersonate legitimate users directly through their verified phone numbers. Consequently, compromised accounts can be used automatically to send fraudulent messages and malicious attachments to secondary contacts. The advisory identifies unexpected messages or official-looking files received from known contacts as primary indicators of targeted cyber attacks. Furthermore, unrecognized entries appearing under WhatsApp’s linked devices tab strongly indicate unauthorized account access.
In response to these persistent threats, NCERT advised officials handling sensitive information to refrain completely from using WhatsApp Web on Windows computers. Furthermore, users are urged to terminate suspicious browser sessions immediately and independently verify unexpected attachments before opening them. The agency reiterated that users must never share account passwords, one-time passwords, or verification codes under any circumstances. Additionally, transferring media files received through instant messaging platforms onto official government computers remains strictly prohibited. Consequently, strict compliance with basic digital hygiene protocols remains essential to safeguarding institutional network infrastructure.
To enhance digital defenses, the cybersecurity authority recommends maintaining updated operating systems, web browsers, and enterprise security software. Furthermore, users must enable mandatory multi-factor authentication across official accounts and activate WhatsApp’s native two-step verification feature. In the event of suspected system compromise, users should immediately disconnect affected devices from local internet networks. Furthermore, system administrators should preserve suspicious messages and technical system logs to assist cybersecurity forensic investigations. Consequently, technical support teams remain on high alert to contain potential network intrusions across public sector institutions.
Read More: WhatsApp warns its users about a serious crashing virus
Cybersecurity experts emphasize that human error remains the primary entry vector for sophisticated social engineering and spear-phishing campaigns. Therefore, public and private organizations are actively organizing digital awareness workshops to train staff on recognizing malicious emails. Meanwhile, federal agencies continue monitoring network traffic to identify host IP addresses associated with known cybercrime syndicates. Authorities confirmed that protecting critical national information infrastructure remains a top national security priority amidst rising cyber threats. Ultimately, continuous system updates and strict password management protocols provide essential protection against evolving digital risks.

articles.title: Alastair Crooke: The ‘War of Grand Design’ - Consortium News
articles.summary: Alastair Crooke: The ‘War of Grand Design’  Consortium News
articles.full_text:
To preserve its supremacy, Washington is pushing Europe to the front line against Russia, even at the risk of nuclear escalation.
By Alastair Crooke
Forum Geopolitica 
The paradigm shifts. The networked supra-national stratum that long has pursued its global “grand design” through manufacturing public consent for wars of imposed compliance has, at last, run up against the limits to power. We are, indeed, at an “emperor has no clothes” moment. All can see it.
Its traditional tools — the U.S. military, the dollar system, the credit trap, the Bretton Woods structures, shock economic therapy and currency wars — are failing to preserve the U.S. élite weltanschauung wherein it would be “unimaginable” that the U.S., having won the Cold War, were to face a world in which the U.S. did not continue to dictate the blueprint.
“In the golden light of an Athens evening, with the Acropolis over his shoulder,” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, on Oct. 7, openly praised colonialism; he engaged in egregious erasures of history, and demanded a return to Western domination of the world. Rubio asserted that the West must use military force to “maintain its place at the head of the world;” the West is “the greatest civilization in the world,” he declared, emphasizing that it is a “civilization that we must fight to defend today with the same passion as our forefathers did.”
But now, those traditional tools to preserve its place at the head of the world are proving less effective against states that possess alternatives — China, Russia and Iran are clear pointers to the trend that economic, financial and even kinetic wars are failing to produce quick results. Quick victories for the Matrix are no longer so readily available.
To suggest, on the other hand, that civilisational states could stand up to the U.S. more forcefully ignores everything about the deep nature of this conflict. The “One Global Government Grand Design,” is a war to eliminate those Civilisational States that offer a different consciousness through which to view and understand the world.
What does that mean? It was former British Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli, who in 1846 inferred — “The world is governed by very different personages from what is imagined by those who are not behind the scenes.”
Disraeli repeatedly explicitly warned against “world revolution” (or colour revolutions in today’s vernacular). Disraeli saw and repeatedly “called out” “a design” behind the series of revolution eruptions that had occurred in many parts of the world at the time in the mid 1800s.
Today it is Emmanuel Todd, the respected French historian and anthropologist, who is echoing Disraeli: Todd sees too in today’s wars something far more profound than a series of separated and distinct territorial conflicts.
Moscow is not waging war against the 20-million odd inhabitants of Ukraine —
“It is confronting, through Ukraine, the entire Atlanticist bloc, NATO as a whole, its intelligence services, its arsenals, its satellites, its military industry, and its media machine. Ukraine is merely a theatre of operations, a battlefield in a latent world war.”
Ukraine, Iran, Yemen or China — all are mere theatres of operations; one battlefield amongst many (occurring in hybrid space) related only through their being swept into a latent world war.
For Todd, today’s wars are a civilizational clash between a declining West and a Russia defending a more traditional, more sovereign, conception of political and social order. Wolfgang Münchau suggests that Ukraine and the Iran-Middle East wars plausibly might merge into a single war — the geopolitical rivalry between China and the U.S. remaining as the primordial conflict of our times.
Emmanual Todd has pointed out that the West, despite its apparent economic and technological superiority, is showing signs of profound fragility — an aging demography, a crisis of confidence, deindustrialization and a loss of ideological bearings.
For decades, as Mattias Forsgren has written,
“The Western core has lived off financialization and the systematic offshoring of production. Industrial capacity was relocated to low-wage countries while the metropolitan economies shifted toward rent extraction, asset inflation and the recycling of global savings through the dollar system. The near-collapse of 2008 exposed how close this structure had come to the abyss… The Covid years repeated the pattern on a greater scale. The structural problems remain unresolved. What has been constructed however, is a more leveraged and fragile system.”
This leveraged financial system is now vulnerable to a potentially crippling financial crisis.
Until 2022, when Europe chose to throw its hand in with Ukraine, Europe’s ruling strata was a party to this “Grand Design” project, led by the “global-government” power bloc. Europe’s ruling strata still is in thrall to “the design.” But in this Trumpian era, it is no longer a full partner. Today, the reality is that America cannot risk vertical escalation to all-out war vis-à-vis its competitors to conserve its global primacy. Its military is too depleted and dysfunctional.
In reaction, opponents such as Russia and Iran have chosen a more subtle, slower, but also far more ambitious strategy, Todd suggests. It is one that combines military pressure, economic warfare, diplomatic battles, geopolitical influence and information warfare. The goal is not just to win militarily, but to durably reshape the world order.
To manage this changed paradigm of war, the U.S. is unloading the “vertical confrontation aspect” onto proxies:
“The European Continent is being transformed from ally into a resource: economically drained, politically captured and militarily prepared as the theatre in which the costs of imperial repair can be paid” (Forsgren).
The ultimate expression of the U.S.’ strategy is a managed escalation of confrontation that keeps the American homeland as sanctuary, whilst Europe absorbs both the conventional attrition and the nuclear risk.
By continuing to act as a willing proxy — through continuing to supply missiles and drones to Ukraine for launch deep into Russia, Europe must expect Russian retaliation — albeit carefully modulated against vulnerable European “assets.” Nonetheless, Europe would then be at war with Russia — a war that, as Wolfgang Münchau acknowledges, Europe is not in a position to win —
“Whose bond markets are going to be blown up first? Who is going to run out of interceptor missiles first? Thanks to the much maligned Common Agricultural Policy, Europe is not going to run out of food. But on every other count — military, energy, finance — Europe is at a disadvantage.”
Since Europe lacks the conventional military resources to mount any decisive escalation of its own, then nuclear weapons risk appearing as the only available “quick fix.”
The mantra that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s nuclear threats are a “bluff” principally serves to lower the psychological caution to European escalation — an escalation that could risk provoking Moscow to perceive little option other than to resort to tactical nuclear weapons as the means to restore credibility to the Russian nuclear deterrent.
In such context — and with U.S.’ escalatory potential largely expended — the U.S. almost certainly would not be ready to put on the table the risk that U.S. cities might be nuked as conflict escalates.
“U.S. tactical nuclear weapons were planned for use inside Europe, against forces on European soil, precisely to keep any nuclear exchange geographically limited,” Forsgren argues —
“Thus the masters of the ‘Design’ strategy aim to corner Russia into a position where its only alternatives are strategic retreat — or, the destruction of Europe as a proxy — a destruction that would nonetheless come at the price to Russia of the damage European nuclear weapons would inflict on Russian territory and forces … whilst all along the American homeland and its financial superstructure stays out of range.”
Forsgren suggests —
“The calculation appears to be, that by gradually raising the level of pressure — keeping Russia inside the zone of zugzwang without crossing into open strategic nuclear exchange — the United States security strata hopes to force Moscow to back down – rather than accept the costs of a wider war.”
The aim has not changed over many decades — it is to compel Russian capitulation. Such a scenario would represent one “theatre of operations” removed in the ultimate proxy conflict to subordinate China to “the Design.”
“The more Europe is positioned as a disposable nuclear front, the sharper the dilemma becomes. The practical effect is to place the entire European continent — and Russian decision-making — on a hair-trigger.”
Europeans must surely realise how they are being used to corral Russia into a war that neither it, nor ordinary Europeans want. Yet having so zealously embraced the Ukraine conflict as a “virtuous” totem around which all fractious European parties could gather, they could well face economic and political catastrophe if Europe continues on its present course of provoking Russia.
“Doubling-down,” as the Europeans seem intent on doing, is no strategy. Their fear-mongering about (imagined) Russian hybrid aggression easily can become a self-fulfilling narrative — leading precisely to an accidental European hot war naively conceived by some in the western security space as the means by which to corner Russia and force its capitulation.
We are at the point where the European political class simply will not allow the topic of war to be aired openly. European elites cling to their strategic denial that Ukraine is losing its war with Russia. Yet the U.S. and Europe teeter at the brink of a bond market collapse, and face clear evidence that their only weapon against Russia — sanctions — has never worked.

articles.full_text:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has mocked Donald Trump’s special envoy after Steve Witkoff described Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian”.
The US representative stunned international allies when he praised the wartime dictator during a face-to-face meeting in St Petersburg last week.
American delegates were meant to be putting forward their latest plan to secure peace in Ukraine for the Kremlin’s consideration.
It came after a particularly alarming few weeks where the US started to fully align itself completely with Russia, apparently forgetting how the Ukraine war began when Putin invaded back in 2022.
Trump agreed to a sanctions-busting diesel deal with Putin, called for Zelenskyy to be ousted as Ukraine’s president, ignored Russia’s repeated breaches of the US’s “energy ceasefire” and was accused of restricting Kyiv’s access to US intelligence.
Witkoff then added salt to the wound when he told Putin: “You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian.
“You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that, I commend you, and I thank you again.”
Asked to respond to the US claim that Ukraine is not “grateful” for the help it has received so far from America, Zelenskyy told ABC News: “They have a right to say what they think about what they want.”
“You don’t get insulted when people say that?” Journalist James Longman asked.
“No, of course – yes,” the Ukrainian president said. “I’m a normal person.
“Maybe not such a big humanitarian as Putin, of course, we are different.
“But in any way, I try my best, really.”
Zelenskyy also said Trump is “cautious” over the phone, but when asked if Trump was “polite”, Zelenskyy hesitated and joked: “Up to you!”
“Like between friends, like in the family, you have to be honest, not to play games. I don’t play games with Trump,” the Ukrainian leader said.
“This is my difference between me and Putin. I don’t play with him any games. I’m direct, honest.”
Zelenskyy said he does not feel betrayed by the US – despite saying otherwise recently – but did express sadness over the lack of US assistance.
“I feel what I feel. It’s not supportive,” he said.

articles.full_text:
Hundreds of protesters stormed the Roman Colosseum and clashed with police at the historic gates as the demonstrations in France spread to Italy over the weekend.
The protesters, many of them young and waving Palestinian flags, were seen cheering and yelling inside the 2,000-year-old arena during the demonstrations in Rome as security forces pushed them out.
The tense scene was one of many across the country on Saturday as thousands marched in the streets of Rome, Milan, Turin and other cities to protest the current cost-of-living crisis and the ongoing war in Gaza.
The Colosseum had notably upped its security ahead of the protest following months of clashes with tourists running wild in the historic site, with the arena declared a security “red zone” last month.
Along with the clashes at the Colosseum, officials reported another violent confrontation with protesters near the Piazza della Repubblica, with police deploying tear gas and water cannons.
In Milan, protesters dumped manure outside the country’s energy regulator and burned an oversized electricity bill.
Many stores in the city boarded up their windows to avoid last week’s looting where protesters were caught making off with luxury goods in France.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni sent about 500 soldiers to Milan to assist the 5,000 officers deployed to the area.
The soldiers, however, were not equipped with pepper spray or Tasers, only plastic restraint ties to help arrest rowdy protesters, Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said.
The protests in Italy mimic the demonstrations that broke out in France last month and have spread across Europe over the continent’s economic woes.

articles.title: Israel committing crimes against humanity in occupied West Bank: UN - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Israel committing crimes against humanity in occupied West Bank: UN  Al JazeeraIsrael Has Committed Genocidal Acts in Gaza Since Cease-Fire, U.N. Human Rights Panel Says  The New York TimesUN inquiry says Israel kept committing genocide in Gaza after truce  Reuters'Legitimazes Jihad': Foreign Affairs Ministry slams UN report accusing Israel of genocide  The Jerusalem PostUN-commissioned experts say Gaza ceasefire has not stopped Israel from committing geno...
articles.full_text:
A United Nations commission of inquiry has accused Israel of committing crimes against humanity in the occupied West Bank, including extermination, torture and rape, while also continuing “to commit genocide in Gaza” despite a ceasefire brokered by the United States.
The report, published on Monday by the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, examined killings and physical and mental harm inflicted by state actors from October 7, 2023, through September of this year.
It was released the day before Israel’s general election.
The commission found that the situation in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967, had “deteriorated gravely” since the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on October 7, 2023.
It said Israeli military operations, reinforced by sustained violence by settlers, amounted to a “widespread and systematic attack” on civilians, and that Israeli authorities “intended to collectively punish” residents of the occupied West Bank for the Hamas-led attack on Israel.
“The Israeli authorities and forces have committed the crimes against humanity of extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence in the West Bank, as well as persecution based on intersecting discriminatory grounds, with nationality, race and ethnicity at its core,” the report said.
Extermination
The commission also found a sharp rise in deaths from air strikes in the territory.
Six Palestinians were killed in air attacks in the occupied West Bank from 2008 to October 6, 2023, it said, compared with 254 from October 7, 2023, to September 30, 2026.
“The intentional killing and injuring of Palestinian civilians and destruction of homes in the West Bank combined with Israel’s persistent denial of responsibility form part of a broader strategy to exterminate and displace Palestinians and impose conditions of life that are unlivable,” said Srinivasan Muralidhar, the commission’s chair.
“Meanwhile, Israel’s expansion of territorial control in Gaza continues to result in the killing and harming of Palestinian civilians who approach or cross” the so-called Yellow Line that demarcates Israeli-controlled areas in the enclave, he said.
Israel’s mission in Geneva called the report part of the commission’s “misinformation campaign to demonize the State of Israel and portray its very existence as criminal”.
“The international community must reject these distortions, repudiate the commission’s findings and demand its immediate dissolution,” the mission said in a statement.
Continued genocide
The commission, which does not speak for the UN as a whole, first concluded in September 2025 that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza during the war that followed the October 7 attacks. Israel has flatly rejected the UN commission’s finding.
In its new report, the commission said Israeli forces had continued to commit “genocidal acts” against Palestinians in Gaza despite the ceasefire brokered by the US last October, with attacks intended to “destroy the Palestinian people, in whole or in part”.
At least five Palestinians, including a seven-year-old girl, were killed in Israeli air attacks across Gaza on Monday, according to medical officials there. The Gaza Health Ministry says at least 74,500 people have been killed in the genocidal war, which has displaced nearly all of the territory’s population.
The report also examined abuses by Palestinian security forces. It found that the Palestinian Authority had targeted people who voiced dissent, and that the killing and wounding of journalists and human rights defenders had steadily narrowed space for civil society.
The three-member commission was established by the UN Human Rights Council in 2021.
Navi Pillay, a former South African High Court judge who led it until last November, won the Nobel Peace Prize this month.
West Bank lockdown
The report was released as Israeli forces carried out a crackdown in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron after a shooting near the city last week. Israel imposed a lockdown on Hebron on Friday, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced plans to extend it across the entire West Bank.
Later on Monday, Volker Turk, the UN high commissioner for human rights, condemned the Hebron operation. He said threats to empty and erase neighbourhoods raised “serious concerns of ethnic cleansing”.
According to Turk, the lockdown had already forcibly displaced more than 2,000 Palestinians, led to the demolition of homes and prevented residents from moving freely.
“The sweeping steps taken raise grave concerns of unnecessary and disproportionate use of force – which must end,” he said.
“The Israeli lockdown is confining many to their homes and their immediate neighbourhoods. Declarations by senior Israeli government officials indicate that the measures implemented are punitive in nature and designed to instil fear. This is unacceptable,” Turk added.
Some Israeli ministers have previously called for the occupied West Bank and Gaza to be ethnically cleansed.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich told Ynet News last month that Israel should “go to war” in the occupied territory and repeat what it “did in Gaza”. He added that Israeli forces had “cleared out” Palestinian refugee camps in the occupied West Bank.
Turk insisted that people displaced under the clampdown must be allowed to return home and that “Israel must ensure compensation and reparation for unlawful evictions and demolitions”.
“Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law,” he said.

articles.full_text:
The Black Sea has become the world’s deadliest shipping route in 2026, with more than 570 vessels struck and at least 40 sailors killed since the beginning of the year, surpassing the Persian Gulf in both the number of attacks and maritime fatalities.
According to the Financial Times on October 25, citing maritime security company Ambrey and the International Maritime Organization, attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea have reached levels more than six times higher than those recorded in the Persian Gulf, where 24 sailor deaths have been confirmed.
The situation deteriorated sharply during the summer. Between July and September, 387 vessels were struck—more than five times the number recorded in the previous quarter. Ambrey estimates that Russia was responsible for approximately 90% of attacks on shipping over the past 45 days.
The latest incidents have extended beyond Ukrainian waters. On October 23, a tanker was struck near Romania’s coast, leaving one sailor dead and three others missing. Earlier, on October 15, drones struck two chemical tankers near Romania, including the Wine Trader and Yara J.
The escalation has significantly disrupted operations at Ukraine’s Greater Odesa ports. According to port operator TIS, fewer than 10 ships passed through the ports last month, compared with approximately 400 in July.
Shipping companies are also facing rising insurance costs. The Financial Times reported that war-risk insurance premiums could reach 15% of a vessel’s hull value, nearly twice the rate for ships operating in the Persian Gulf.
As a result, some operators have withdrawn from Black Sea routes, while others are deploying older vessels, some up to 50 years old, to reduce insurance expenses.
The disruption has also affected Ukraine’s agricultural exports. Maritime shipments fell to 1.4 million tonnes in August, approximately 75% below prewar levels, while continued attacks on ports have complicated efforts to redirect exports through the Danube.

articles.title: Pentagon orders bases to plan for 90 days without the grid as Britain urges families to stockpile food and water - Fortune
articles.summary: Pentagon orders bases to plan for 90 days without the grid as Britain urges families to stockpile food and water  FortuneInside the Pentagon's doomsday plan to keep America fighting if global war erupts  Fox NewsPentagon Starting with Resilient Energy for Sweeping ‘FORTRESS America’ Project  Air & Space Forces MagazinePentagon’s FORTRESS Plan Prepares US Bases to Operate 90 Days Without Outside Support  UNITED24 MediaUnder Pentagon’s Doomsday Scenario, F.E...
articles.full_text:
The Pentagon wants every major U.S. military base to run for 90 days without outside help if a war cuts off power and supply chains. Across the Atlantic, Britain is telling families to keep canned food, bottled water and cash on hand to get through three days of disruption.
The two efforts aren’t known to be coordinated, and neither government has said a new war is imminent. But both are planning for disruptions that could leave homes and military installations without the services they depend on.
Inside the Pentagon’s 90-day plan
The Pentagon is developing a requirement that every major military installation in the continental U.S. be able to sustain essential operations on its own for at least 90 days, Fox News Digital reported Oct. 25, citing internal planning documents. The requirement falls under an initiative called FORTRESS, short for Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth unveiled FORTRESS in his Sept. 30 “State of the Force” address. He pledged that every major installation would generate its own power, independent of the civilian grid. A follow-up memo laid out plans for a dedicated program office. The 90-day standard goes further than that original goal, extending self-sufficiency beyond electricity to water, fuel and communications.
The plan envisions portable nuclear reactors, large-scale battery storage and microgrids that can disconnect bases from civilian power networks. The Army has already moved in that direction: In August it announced up to $2.2 billion in awards to build nuclear microreactors at five bases, including Fort Bragg and Fort Hood.
“Power is combat now,” Pentagon chief spokesperson Sean Parnell, who Fox said led the FORTRESS initiative, told the outlet. “Without electricity, you lose communications, water, logistics, assembly lines and just basic military command structures.”
FORTRESS also calls for strategic reserves of munitions, fuel, critical minerals, electronics, spare parts and medical supplies. For the military’s most critical dependencies, it would require at least two qualified supply or production pathways, so that losing a single factory or supplier wouldn’t halt operations.
Through the Civil Reserve Manufacturing Network, an existing program folded into FORTRESS, the Pentagon plans to identify commercial factories that could switch to defense production in a crisis. Technical specifications, cybersecurity protections, contracting arrangements and conversion procedures would be worked out in advance.
The threat no one names out loud
The Pentagon hasn’t publicly identified a specific country as FORTRESS’s target. But in a February 2024 joint advisory, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, NSA and FBI warned that Chinese state-sponsored hackers known as Volt Typhoon had compromised IT networks of U.S. organizations in the communications, energy, transportation and water sectors. The agencies said the hackers were potentially positioning themselves to disrupt essential services during a future conflict. Microsoft first flagged the group’s activity in 2023.
The Pentagon hasn’t released a cost estimate or timeline. A senior defense official told reporters Oct. 20 that officials are still assessing the needs of roughly 500 bases in the continental U.S. and that fully meeting the goal could take decades, according to Air & Space Forces Magazine. The magazine estimated the cost could run into the tens of billions of dollars, if not hundreds of billions.
Britain tells families to prepare for 3 days without essential services
Details of the Pentagon plan emerged days after the British government launched its Be Ready campaign on Oct. 22.
The government’s checklist recommends three liters of drinking water per person per day. It also lists nonperishable food that needs no cooking or refrigeration, flashlights, power banks, first-aid supplies, a battery-powered or wind-up radio, and food and water for pets. Households are also encouraged to keep cash in case card payments and ATMs go down.
The government describes Be Ready as the first stage of a three-year campaign covering severe weather and other emergencies. Britain has published household preparedness guidance since May 2024, so the campaign isn’t a sudden signal that war is near.
Britain’s defense leadership has been far blunter. Writing in The Telegraph over the weekend, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting warned that adversaries could have the force strength and war economy to attack by 2030. That leaves Britain and its NATO allies a little over 1,000 days to prepare, he wrote.
“To prevent the worst, we have to prepare for it,” Streeting wrote. He pointed to threats from hostile states, cyberattacks, organized crime and climate change, and argued that terms like “hybrid warfare” understate the danger.
Russia, China and Iran are already probing British systems
The concerns aren’t new. Britain’s 2025 National Security Strategy named Russia the country’s most acute threat and flagged Iranian hostile activity. It also cast China as a sophisticated, persistent challenge and highlighted undersea cables, energy pipelines and transportation networks as infrastructure to protect.
A July government resilience report pointed to new conflict in the Middle East, a growing number of sub-threshold attacks from Russia and several major cyberattacks.
Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre handled more than 200 cyber incidents affecting critical infrastructure and its supporting ecosystem between June 2025 and May 2026. NCSC chief executive Richard Horne said in June that about 75% of those incidents were believed to be linked to state actors, naming Russia, China and Iran.
Britain isn’t alone
In March 2025, the European Commission unveiled a preparedness strategy calling for guidelines to help EU residents keep at least 72 hours of emergency supplies.
In the U.S., President Trump marked FEMA’s National Preparedness Month in September, an annual campaign dating to 2004, with a presidential message. He urged Americans to keep emergency kits, know their evacuation routes and ready themselves for “natural and man-made threats.”
Emergency preparedness is nothing new. But the latest push comes as Western governments grow more worried about cyberattacks, sabotage and other forms of hybrid warfare linked to Russia, China and Iran. The next conflict may not start on a battlefield. It could start with the power going out.
