articles.title: Mecca defence alliance members in Tehran to defuse Iran-US, Yemen tensions - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Mecca defence alliance members in Tehran to defuse Iran-US, Yemen tensions  Al JazeeraIran hosts Saudi Arabia and regional powers as fears grow of return to war  CNNOil ticks lower as Saudi defense minister meets with Iran's president in Tehran to de-escalate  CNBCSaudi defence pact countries push for peace in Tehran as Houthis launch more attacks  ReutersIran hosts regional powers for talks to prevent fresh escalation  Financial Times
articles.full_text:
Tehran, Iran – Ministers and senior security officials from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye – the three nations that signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement – are in Tehran to discuss regional security issues amid threats of new US strikes on Iran.
Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman Al Saud, Pakistani military chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian and will discuss tensions with security chief Mohsen Rezaei.
The meetings are among the highest-profile dialogues held in Tehran in recent months. While there is still little information on what might be discussed, the meetings come amid a flurry of diplomatic activity to deal with a new escalation between the United States and Iran.
“The Mecca pact’s 11th-hour visit to Tehran is an attempt to tip the balance in favour of those willing to compromise before the guns start blazing again,” said Ali Vaez, deputy director of the Middle East and North Africa Program at the International Crisis Group.
“But unless they arrive with a credible formula to bridge the US-Iran divide, they may find themselves with little more than goodwill in a race against the clock.”
The talks are expected to address the waves of missile and drone attacks carried out by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, who are allied with Tehran, on Saudi Arabia, which supports Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
“I believe that parties to the Mecca agreement lack options of military engagement with the Houthis, but Riyadh is certainly asserting greater pressure for more, and its expectation of its partners has grown in parallel with the offensive from Yemen,” Ayesha Siddiqa, a senior research fellow in the Department of War Studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.
But despite the collective security arrangement in the Mecca defence pact, Saudi Arabia’s allies Turkiye and Pakistan cannot “afford to commit troops on the ground” in Yemen, said Siddiqa.
The latest diplomatic push is likely linked to visits by Pakistani army chief Asim Munir to Saudi Arabia and Iran last week, Siddiqa said, and coincides with Islamabad’s restrictions on overland border trade with Tehran amid the US blockade on Iran.
Iranian authorities have said they favoured “security originating from within the region” as they prepared for the meetings.
Umer Karim, who researches Saudi foreign policy and its implications for regional security, said the Tehran meetings are unlikely to reduce the risk of a renewed war between Iran and the US, which would likely lead to more regional turmoil.
“Therefore, these talks perhaps are more concerned about the security of Saudi Arabia and involve an attempt by Turkiye and Pakistan to compel Iran to reach a compromise,” he told Al Jazeera.
Sanam Vakil, the director of Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa programme, said she was “cautiously optimistic” about the impact of the immediate meeting, but “less positive” about a lasting breakthrough.
“Iran has strong incentives to avoid another major confrontation, and there may be room for limited understandings, particularly concerning Yemen,” she said. “However, the Houthis have their own calculations, and Iran’s influence over them is not absolute. Preventing renewed US-Israeli attacks will be even more difficult because the fundamental disagreements between Tehran and Washington remain unresolved.”
US President Donald Trump is said to be considering new attacks to break the diplomatic deadlock with Iran, which has refused to agree to any peace agreement with Washington unless several of its demands are met.
The US and regional powers want international shipping and transit through the Strait of Hormuz to resume without impediments or attacks. Washington also wants to rein in Tehran’s nuclear programme and bring in international inspectors to assess Iran’s highly enriched uranium. Israel says it wants to overthrow the Islamic Republic.
Tehran wants to lift the US naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports, which has halted crude oil exports and disrupted most trade, and return to a memorandum of understanding agreed between the two countries in June.
The US has refused this, with President Trump saying he is left with a choice to “finish the job” by launching major strikes on Iran’s civilian infrastructure. This could prompt Iran to lash out at its neighbours, as it did earlier in the war with strikes on US bases in Arab states and infrastructure.
Meanwhile, the US Department of State issued an October 21 order for nonemergency US government employees and their family members to leave Saudi Arabia for their safety’s sake, given the Houthi threat.
As talks involving Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye continue in Iran, analysts say these Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signatories will likely try to minimise the impact on Saudi Arabia if war does break out again.
“However, since little has changed from an Iranian strategic calculus and the actors involved don’t have the kind of leverage needed to affect Iran’s strategic thinking, these negotiations are going to yield little,” Karim said.

Donald Trump launched a 1,300-word social media rant against the late-night US TV host Bill Maher on Sunday evening, calling him a “TOTAL LOSER” in a fresh assault on the media.
“Let’s talk about this COMPLETE AND TOTAL LOSER, Bill Maher,” the US president wrote. “He’s got a Low Rated Show on equally Low Rated HBO, which was once, long ago, a Network of Quality and Excitement – But that’s all gone.”

Trump’s lengthy and detailed post about Maher came after the host interviewed Karoline Leavitt, the former White House press secretary, on his program Real Time with Bill Maher.
Maher asked Leavitt about Trump’s “lame duck” presidency and whether the president would act on “vengeance” if Republicans largely lose to Democrats in next week’s midterms.
“I worry that if this election goes as badly as it looks like it’s going to go for him and the Republicans, we’re going to have a guy who doesn’t have as much power as he did … and we know he likes vengeance,” Maher told Leavitt.
But Leavitt remained steadfast in her support for Trump and expressed confidence that Republicans could still outperform expectations.
Trump called Maher a “coward who is afraid to tell the truth about how well our Country is running”, claiming that Maher praised him behind the scenes but on television insults him with jokes.
“Also, turn your Laugh Machine off, it’s a joke when they laugh uncontrollably, even when you say nothing funny, and I’m going to have the Republicans not cover you anymore, because they try to talk about you as a guy who is transformative,” Trump wrote.
Trump has previously insulted late-night hosts and comedians on his platform and taken personal offense at those who make him the punchline. Earlier this year, Trump called for Jimmy Kimmel’s show to be terminated after the ABC late-night host joked about Melania Trump. Last year, the US president also called for Seth Meyers to be fired.
But Trump’s lengthy attack on Maher is notable, coming just about a week until the US midterm elections, where Republicans are trying to fend off challenges from Democratic opponents.
The US president chose to launch a tirade against Maher as public polling shows Americans are growing increasingly unhappy with Trump’s handling of the US economy, cost of living and war with Iran.
But Trump chose to dispute several specific talking points Maher made on his show, including the host’s comments about the justice department’s efforts to target ballots they claim were cast by noncitizens in California, rumors that Trump is turning the White House press briefing room into a swimming pool and Trump’s endorsement of Republican candidates in the upcoming midterms.
Maher, who has been described as a moderate liberal, has dined with Trump on two occasions during the US president’s second administration. Maher has shared his experience with Trump on his HBO show.
Among other insults Trump launched at Maher, he accused the host of drinking a lot of alcohol when they dined together, being a “POTHEAD”, not being nice and catering to a base of viewers who “don’t like working”.

Russian refiners have raised diesel output for October after Moscow issued export quotas under the Kremlin’s supply agreement with the United States, two industry sources told Reuters on Monday. Daily production fell to about 160,000 metric tons in the first half of the month, from 175,000 tons in September. It began climbing toward 180,000 tons a day once the quotas arrived in mid-October.
Russia’s domestic diesel consumption typically drops to about 140,000 tons a day in October, after the grain harvest and the summer driving season end, leaving at least 40,000 tons a day, more than 1 million tons a month, available for export, according to the sources. Between 200,000 and 300,000 tons of that is likely to go to neighbouring countries under intergovernmental agreements.
Moscow is expected to keep its diesel export ban, which took effect in August, in place and to use quotas to control how much leaves the country.
U.S. President Donald Trump said on October 9 that Russia would ship more than 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons after that. A further 3 million tons would depend on the condition of Russia’s refineries. Washington has temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian fuel to allow the trade, with a six-month Treasury waiver issued the same day.
The waiver goes beyond pre-election price relief, and is seen by some analysts as a first step toward easing sanctions on Russian energy and pulling Moscow’s supplies back toward the West and away from China, which has come to rely on Russia since the Hormuz closure cut off Gulf oil.
The first cargo on the Malta-flagged Agioi Fanendes left Primorsk on October 23 with about 40,000 tons of ultra-low sulfur diesel and is due in New York on November 7, four days after the midterm elections. The average U.S. diesel price stood at $6.32 a gallon that day, up from $3.63 a year earlier.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said shipments to the United States would continue regularly. At least two other tankers carrying Russian diesel have signaled destinations in Turkey and Brazil.
Analysts doubt the volumes will move the market. Standard Chartered has warned that Russia will struggle to raise diesel output in the near term because Ukrainian drone strikes have damaged its refineries, which will take months to repair. The bank adds that barrels redirected to U.S. buyers come out of supply to Russia’s existing customers. Kyiv resumed refinery strikes on October 15 after a three-day pause, which puts the October recovery at risk.

A drone attack reportedly hit a 25-story business center and residential buildings in Russia’s Voronezh, while a separate train derailment in Sverdlovsk Region left seven fuel tankers burning.
The independent Russian outlet Astra reported that a drone struck the Chizhova Gallery business center at 35A Koltsovskaya Street. The complex includes a 25-story high-rise that is one of the city center’s prominent architectural landmarks, according to the facility’s website.
The attack prompted reports of numerous explosions and fires across Voronezh. Astra said a drone threat was declared in the region at around 3 a.m., followed by a missile threat approximately two hours later. Residents told the outlet that they had heard explosions but that no air-raid sirens had sounded.
Residential buildings, vehicles reportedly damaged
An Astra OSINT analysis of photographs and videos identified several locations where damage or fires were reported.
According to the outlet, a residential complex at 4K Arkhitektora Troitskogo Street was struck, while the newly built Uritsky residential complex at 135 Uritskogo Street also sustained damage. The latter building was completed last year, Astra reported.
At least 10 cars were reportedly on fire in a parking area at 275/1 45-y Strelkovoy Divizii Street. The outlet also reported fires in residential areas and smoke spreading across the city.
Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ claimed that some of the impacts resulted from Russian electronic warfare systems operating inside the city, alleging that Russian air defenses caused damage while attempting to counter the drones. The claim has not been independently verified.
Another monitoring channel, Supernova+, reported that the Severny Bridge in Voronezh may also have been targeted, citing reports that the bridge was closed and smoke was visible nearby.
Industrial and aviation facilities possibly targeted
Supernova+, citing their own open-source intelligence analysis, suggested that the Voronezhsintezkauchuk synthetic rubber plant and the Voronezh Aircraft Joint-Stock Company (VASO) may also have been targeted.
Voronezhsintezkauchuk, part of Russian petrochemical group SIBUR, produces synthetic rubber and thermoplastic elastomers. VASO is part of Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation and participates in the production of Il-96 long-haul aircraft and components for other aircraft.
Killed and injured in Voronezh drone attack, governor says
A drone attack reportedly killed two people and injured 17 others in Voronezh.
Voronezh Region Governor Alexander Gusev said the two people killed were men born in 1960 and 1973. One child was among the injured, and two of the wounded were in serious condition.
A significant number of those injured were traveling on a train passing through Voronezh’s left-bank suburbs when drone debris fell onto it, Gusev said. Emergency services were working at the scene.
The attack also sparked fires at several industrial facilities, a business center, an apartment building, two dacha settlements, a school stadium, and a garage cooperative, according to the governor. He said the industrial fires had no major consequences.
Building facades and windows were damaged in nearly every district of the city, Gusev added.
According to the governor, air defense forces shot down more than 70 drones over Voronezh, while 113 were intercepted across the metropolitan area and several districts of the region. These figures have not been independently verified.
Neither the Russian defense ministry nor Ukrainian officials have commented on the reported attack.
Freight train derails in Sverdlovsk Region
Separately, 20 freight train cars derailed in Russia’s Sverdlovsk Region, with seven fuel tankers catching fire, according to reports cited by Astra. The cause of the incident has not been disclosed, and no casualties have been reported.
The Sverdlovsk Railway said traffic on the Reshety-Aramil section had been suspended after the derailment compromised clearance of an adjacent track. Firefighting and recovery trains were dispatched to the scene.
Local residents reported seeing flames and thick black smoke, with one witness telling media that an explosion had illuminated the area near the Chusovsky Tract.
Russia’s consumer rights watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said it would test air quality in nearby residential areas.
The derailment comes amid a series of reported disruptions to Russian railway infrastructure in recent months.
The Moscow Times reported that Ukrainian drone attacks on railway infrastructure in the Bryansk Region on Sept. 28 caused 10 railcars to derail after a railway bridge section collapsed, while a separate incident derailed 18 empty freight cars.
Other reported railway incidents in September and July caused train delays and damage, although the causes differed.
Neither Russian nor Ukrainian officials have publicly attributed the Sverdlovsk derailment to an attack.

articles.title: ‘It’s collective punishment’: nearly 2,000 Palestinians in Hebron displaced as Israeli forces take over homes - The Guardian
articles.summary: ‘It’s collective punishment’: nearly 2,000 Palestinians in Hebron displaced as Israeli forces take over homes  The GuardianIsrael expands expulsions in occupied West Bank to cement control  Al JazeeraIsraeli military closing West Bank crossings ahead of upcoming elections as massive operation continues  CBS NewsWest Bank: Hebron crackdown displaces thousands, Türk warns of ethnic cleansing  UN NewsBulldozers tear down home as Israel cracks down in the West...
articles.full_text:
Hebron, the biggest city in the West Bank, had paid little attention to Israel’s looming elections until it found itself suddenly in the midst of them, a proving ground for Benjamin Netanyahu’s security credentials in the run-up to Tuesday’s vote.
A gun attack on an Israeli military checkpoint on Friday in which two soldiers were killed brought immediate televised visits from Netanyahu and his finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, whose ruling coalition is narrowly trailing with two days of campaigning left.
They vowed abrupt and sweeping retribution, and the prime minister warned of imminent military operations on a scale the West Bank has not seen in nearly 60 years of occupation.
Within hours, the whole city of 250,000 people had been sealed off and the neighbourhood of Farsh al-Hawa, closest to the site of Friday’s attack, had been flattened. By Sunday morning, there was nothing left but rubble of an industrial area that had been full of car workshops, a big ceramics plant and other enterprises.
As the bulldozers were at work there, another district a few kilometres away was being systematically emptied. Ein Deir Baha was allegedly home to at least one of the two men involved in the attack (both of whom were killed on the spot), and on Friday its residents paid the price.
The imam from the local mosque, Fahed Ahmaro, was woken at about midnight by the loudspeakers from military vehicles patrolling the street, telling homeowners to vacate their homes immediately for their own safety.
Ahmaro had 30 members of his family living in his house. He rushed his frail mother and some of his grandchildren to his daughter’s house in another part of Hebron, and was on his way back in the hope of picking up some of his possessions when his neighbour phoned him.
“He told me not to come back, and the army had blown up the gates to the house. I don’t know what they have done to it by now. I heard they destroyed the furniture,” Ahmaro said. “You don’t know what you have until you lose it. Now I realise how devastating it is to lose your home.”
At midday on Sunday, he was in a Hebron market shopping for a change of clothes for his grandchildren, uncertain how long the family’s exile would last.
He had heard that the house was being used as a base by Israeli soldiers and looking up at the house, perched on the side of a steep hill, he could see some lights on but no sign of life.
The Hebron municipality said that 370 families, nearly 2,000 people, had been displaced by the army sweep through Ein Deir Baha. In its official comments, the Israeli army had said that the displaced population had left voluntarily, that “civilians who wished to evacuate were permitted to temporarily leave the area”.
Ahmaro was outraged at the suggestion that he had any choice about fleeing.
“Never, never, never. Why should I leave my house?” he asked.
Abdul Halim al-Tamimi tried to stay put when the military came at 1.30am. The 77-year-old was told his family had only 10 minutes to vacate their home.
“An intelligence officer told me if we didn’t go, they would displace us the same way they have done it in Gaza,” he said. “We stood there in front of the house, and we refused to leave until we were faced by three military vehicles and they forced us out.”
By the time the Tamimi family left, it was 3am on Saturday morning. On Sunday morning their home was festooned with large Israeli flags and ringed with military vehicles. The army had turned the substantial villa into its headquarters.
In its statement, the Israeli military claimed that 2,000 local people were from the Jaba’a clan, from which the gunmen were allegedly drawn, and which the army claimed was “associated with Hamas”.
The claim drew consternation and derision from people in Ein Deir Baha. They numbered the extent of the Jaba’a clan at 150 at most, with no known reputation for radicalism.
“We are from a completely different family. We are innocent people. We have nothing to do with the whole thing,” Tamimi said. “I don’t know what they are using it for, other than maybe election publicity.”
Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have no vote in Tuesday’s elections, but their lives could be deeply affected by the outcome.
By Sunday evening, all roads in and out of the city remained closed to cars, with heavy steel barriers swung across them. The only traffic was on foot, with taxi drivers squabbling for fares. The driver of a delivery truck, Wasam Sadi, pulled in at one checkpoint with the cab windshield smashed and glass fragments in his eyes. He had been attacked by settlers at a nearby junction, he said.
“It’s collective punishment,” said Hebron’s mayor, Yousef al-Jabari. “They have dragged people from their houses, and they have prevented the media from getting into the district in order to cover up what is happening.
“Netanyahu and his gang are using Palestinian land to displace Palestinian people, closing the city, closing the mosque, in order to achieve their political goals.”

articles.title: [Arctic Maritime Strategy] NATO’s Northern Defense: Russia’s Northern Fleet and the GIUK Gap - https://economy.ac/
articles.summary: [Arctic Maritime Strategy] NATO’s Northern Defense: Russia’s Northern Fleet and the GIUK Gap  https://economy.ac/
articles.full_text:
Authored On
Modified
Kalibr-armed submarines can strike Europe without crossing the gap
NATO’s sensors, aircraft and frigates still lag the threat
Denmark’s patrol gap leaves the Denmark Strait thinly covered
In the two years leading up to December 2025, Russian vessels threatening UK waters increased by 30%. The UK Ministry of Defence announced this when London and Oslo signed the Lunna House Agreement. The same announcement named the Yantar, a Russian intelligence ship found lurking off the northern coast of the UK near Scotland and tracked by P-8s from Lossiemouth. Earlier, in October, HMS Iron Duke escorted the submarine Novorossiysk through the English Channel while the submarine was sailing on the surface. None of this would have shocked a Cold War sonar operator. For 40 years Soviet subs were in these waters and NATO had hydrophones deployed across the sea floor from Greenland to Iceland to Scotland. What has changed is what the GIUK Gap has to protect. This is why the GIUK Gap has once again become a focus of NATO’s Northern defense.
How the Kola Peninsula Connects to the GIUK Gap
The Kola Peninsula is Russia’s base for its Northern Fleet, located along the Arctic coast just east of Norway. The North Atlantic Current still keeps the water warm enough that it does not freeze during the winter. The Russian Northern Fleet is headquartered in Severomorsk, just outside Murmansk and Russia’s latest attack submarines are stationed in Zapadnaya Litsa, the furthest west submarine base on the Kola Peninsula and close to the Norwegian border. The only way out of the Kola Peninsula into open ocean is to travel West through the Barents Sea, past North Cape and Bear Island. Then travel southwest into the Norwegian Sea. The Norwegian Sea is located between Norway on its East end and Jan Mayen and Iceland to the West. South of the Norwegian Sea, the seabed begins to rise towards Greenland, Iceland, the Faroe Islands and Shetland. So, a submarine would have to pass through the Denmark Strait or between Iceland and the Faroes or the Faroes and Shetland.
These are the gaps that make up the GIUK Gap. South of them lie the trade routes that would be used to send American troops to Europe in a war, as well as cables and pipelines that, according to the UK Ministry of Defence, carry communications, power and gas to Britain and Norway. NATO considers the Arctic to be an entrance to the North Atlantic, connecting North America to Europe with trade, transport and communication. In the Cold War, this worked. The Soviet Union would keep its ballistic missile submarines safe in the Barents Sea while it tried to send attack submarines through the GIUK Gap to attack ships. NATO would use its hydrophones on the sea floor, P-3s out of Keflavik and its own submarines to intercept them.
Today that is no longer the case. The Russian Yasen-M submarine can fire the 3M-54 Kalibr, which has a range of around 1,000 miles, according to USNI News. Attack submarines armed with such missiles can threaten 75 percent of European capitals from the North Sea. If a submarine is in the Norwegian Sea, it does not need to pass through the GIUK Gap to attack the UK or any other country on the European mainland. In August 2026, an article in the German defence magazine Europäische Sicherheit & Technik went into more detail. It said that Russian submarines armed with Kalibr now treat the GIUK Gap as a barrier of their own, keeping U.S. Navy submarines and other large NATO vessels out of the Norwegian Sea. That turns water the Soviets once used as a transit route into a battlefield.
Russia’s Northern Fleet Is Struggling on the Surface While Building Submarines
The strongest case that NATO is overreacting comes from Norway. The Norwegian Intelligence Service’s threat assessment, Focus 2025, states that the war in Ukraine is draining Russia’s Navy, with the Northern Fleet having to decide whether to complete missions or maintain its ships because it does not have enough room in its dockyards to do both. This can also be seen in the Northern Fleet’s surface ships. The nuclear cruiser Admiral Nakhimov has been out of service since 1999 and in July 2026 the commander of the Russian Navy said he hoped to have its modernisation completed in the coming months. These facts would suggest that NATO is spending money on new assets it would have bought anyway and that this talk of the High North is nothing more than new budgets.
However, the Norwegian Intelligence Service stated that submarines have been able to continue their expansion and that it expects the Northern Fleet to send regular deployments into the Atlantic, with 3 or possibly 4 more Borei-As joining within the next few years. Russia has also continued to build its attack submarine force. The Arkhangelsk, the fifth submarine of the Yasen class, was commissioned on 27 December 2024 and deployed to Zapadnaya Litsa. The Perm will be the first submarine designed from the start to carry the Zircon hypersonic missile and the head of the Russian Navy told the Kremlin that he hopes to have it operational by the end of 2026. The Ulyanovsk was launched on 28 July 2026. It can hold up to 32 Zircon missiles and is due to be delivered in December 2027, with another hull laid down in June.
These facts answer the question of whether the Russian Northern Fleet is expanding or NATO is simply meeting it with new technology. The Russian submarine force is smaller than what NATO had to deal with in the 1980s but with each new submarine, Russia can threaten more areas than the Soviet Union could with a larger fleet. NATO is meeting the Russians in the same familiar waters, only with newer technology that can cover the threats. The fact that Russia’s surface fleet is struggling should not deter allies from protecting these waters.
Finding Russian Submarines Takes More Than Patrol Aircraft
Because aircraft can cover a wider area of the ocean, they will always be the most effective way to find submarines. The UK has 9 P-8s based out of Lossiemouth. Norway has 5 based out of Evenes in northern Norway, replacing its old Orion base on Andøya. The U.S. rotates P-8 squadrons through Keflavik. Germany received its first P-8 in November 2025 and is looking to deploy them across the UK, Norway and Iceland. In October 2025, Denmark concluded its Second Agreement on the Arctic and North Atlantic, worth 27.4 billion Danish kroner. This includes acquiring a maritime patrol aircraft capability in cooperation with a NATO ally, as well as 2 new Arctic ships and more drones and follows a first agreement in January 2025 worth 14.6 billion kroner.
Aircraft will always be a short-term solution, because a submarine can just wait for them to leave, so longer-term solutions are needed. The Royal Navy’s Atlantic Bastion concept is one, described in the Ministry of Defence’s Strategic Defence Review from June 2025. It will start with a net of uncrewed vehicles placed in certain areas, probably including the GIUK Gap. This is expected to be run by a private company with the Navy keeping oversight. The Royal Navy hopes to have these sensors in the water during 2026, with the aim of covering the area from the Mid-Atlantic Ridge to the Norwegian Sea. The Lunna House Agreement will see Britain join Norway’s programme to develop motherships for uncrewed mine hunting and undersea warfare systems, as well as working together to bring these autonomous systems to NATO.
Satellites have a smaller role than most would think. They cannot detect submarines, but they can see surface ships, including the Yantar and other ships that support Russia’s Northern Fleet. Satellites are also used to communicate in these higher latitudes, which is why NATO lists the NORTHLINK Arctic satellite project among its new capabilities and the Lunna House Agreement builds on an earlier UK and Norway satellite agreement. In the end, crewed ships are still needed to hunt these submarines. That is what the second stage of Atlantic Bastion does, connecting these sensors to Britain’s Astute-class submarines, P-8s and the new Type 26 frigates, which are designed to hunt submarines. This is what the Lunna House Agreement is trying to achieve with 8 British and at least 5 Norwegian Type 26s. With cheaper sensors, more area can be covered. The only downside is that if these sensors are run by private companies, it is unclear whether they will still be reporting in a crisis.
How NATO Allies Divide the GIUK Gap
NATO has made many changes to its command structure. Joint Force Command Norfolk was created in 2019 and is based in Virginia and one of its main jobs is to keep the sea lanes open between North America and Europe. Its area of responsibility already included Iceland, Norway and the UK and in December 2025 NATO expanded it to include Denmark, Finland and Sweden. JFC Norfolk also leads Arctic Sentry, which began in February 2026. Arctic Sentry gives NATO a better understanding of what its allies are doing in the Arctic and combines these operations with NORAD, U.S. Northern Command, and U.S. European Command. In October 2025 a new Combined Air Operations Centre was established in Bodø, allowing NATO to monitor airspace over the Nordic region, the Baltic Sea, the North Atlantic and the Barents Sea. NATO also established Task Force X-Arctic in June 2026.
Most of these tasks will be broken down among the allies that have coastlines. Norway will be watching the gap closest to the Kola Peninsula, with its P-8s out of Evenes and its intelligence ship Marjata, based out of Kirkenes, watching Russian activity. Britain will be covering the eastern side of the GIUK Gap, as well as the gap between the Faroes and Shetland, where submarines would travel if they wanted to reach the Irish Sea. Through the Lunna House Agreement, Britain and Norway are working together to create a pool of ships that can be used interchangeably, allowing them to share maintenance and technology. articles.title: Iran says nuclear work will continue within NPT framework: Is Tehran planning to leave the treaty? - Business Upturn
articles.summary: Iran says nuclear work will continue within NPT framework: Is Tehran planning to leave the treaty?  Business Upturn
articles.full_text:
Iran said on Monday that its nuclear activities would continue within the framework of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), while President Masoud Pezeshkian reiterated that Tehran is not seeking nuclear weapons. The statement comes amid renewed internal pressure from hardliners to leave the treaty and as diplomacy with the United States remains uncertain.
The message was issued in Tehran on October 26 through Iran’s official ISNA news agency and repeated by government officials. Iran says it retains the right under the NPT to peaceful nuclear energy, research and enrichment for civilian purposes; it denies any ambition to build an atomic bomb. Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei separately said Iran “has neither possessed a nuclear weapon nor ever sought to acquire it.”
Why the statement matters
Iran’s declaration is significant because it pushes back against a hardline faction, the Paydari Front, which has urged parliament and the Supreme National Security Council to begin withdrawing from the NPT. That group argues the treaty has failed to shield Iranian nuclear sites, while moderates around Pezeshkian see continued membership as a legal and diplomatic safeguard.
The dispute matters internationally because the UN nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), has said it cannot fully verify whether Iran has suspended enrichment-related and reprocessing activities. Western governments, including the United States and United Kingdom, have also said Iran remains out of compliance with parts of its NPT safeguards obligations.
What Iran is claiming
Iranian officials frame the latest position as a defence of sovereignty rather than escalation. Iran’s UN Ambassador Gholamhossein Darzi said last week that Tehran had “neither abandoned nor suspended its safeguards obligations,” although he argued that military attacks had altered the security conditions under which they could be implemented.
President Pezeshkian said Iran wants to meet technical and scientific needs and is prepared to assure the world that its programme is peaceful. “We are not looking for nuclear weapons,” he said, while adding that Iran had been forced to change course after the United States withdrew from the 2015 nuclear agreement.
Confirmed facts versus claims
- Confirmed: Iran says its nuclear activities will continue within the NPT framework and that it upholds peaceful-use rights under Article IV of the treaty.
- Confirmed: Pezeshkian and Baghaei have publicly denied that Iran seeks nuclear weapons.
- Claim by Iran: Its nuclear programme is exclusively civilian and its facilities are being unfairly targeted.
- Counter-position: The IAEA and Western governments say verification gaps and enrichment-related activity remain serious concerns.
What happens next
Attention will now turn to whether Iran’s parliament or Supreme National Security Council acts on the Paydari Front’s NPT-withdrawal demand. Any formal move to leave the treaty would sharply raise tensions with the IAEA, the United States and European powers.
Diplomacy has not formally collapsed: Iran’s Foreign Ministry says messages are still being conveyed to Washington through intermediaries. But without restored IAEA access and a credible negotiating framework, Iran’s promise to stay inside the NPT is likely to face mounting political pressure at home.
